# Counting points in thin sets: A survey

**Authors:** Dante Bonolis Address: Duke University, 120 Science Drive, Durham NC 27708 Email address: dante.bonolis@duke.edu , Lillian B. Pierce Address: Duke University, 120 Science Drive, Durham NC 27708 Email address: lillian.pierce@duke.edu and Katharine Woo Address: 450 Serra Mall, Building 380, Stanford CA 94305 Email address: khwoo98@stanford.edu

## Abstract

In the 1980’s Serre asked how many points of bounded height can lie in a thin set. This has motivated significant research ever since, culminating in a series of recent breakthroughs. It is a good time to take stock of the central questions that have been resolved, and also to highlight remaining open questions. First, we survey recent progress on counting points of bounded height in the four types of thin sets, according to the projective/affine and type I/type II designations. Second, we turn to questions of uniformity. Famously, in the setting of type I thin sets, the best-known upper bound for the number of points of bounded height is independent of the maximum size, say $\|F\|$ , of the coefficients of the polynomials that define the thin set; such an upper bound is called uniform. A uniform upper bound in the setting of type II thin sets is not known. For type II thin sets, we explore the dependence on $\|F\|$ via several strategies, and construct counterexamples that suggest the question of uniformity is quite subtle in the setting of type II thin sets.

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. Overview

Circa 1980, Serre formulated the notion of a thin set. A subset $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ is thin if there is an algebraic variety $X$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ and a morphism $\pi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ such that

(i) $M\subset\pi(X(\mathbb{Q}))$ , and

(ii) the fibre of $\pi$ over the generic point is finite and $\pi$ has no rational section over $\mathbb{Q}$ .

A thin set $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ is defined accordingly, with $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ replaced in each instance by $\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ .

This notion was initially recorded in a course of J.-P. Serre in 1980-1981 at the Collège de France, which we cite here in the form [Ser97]. Serre’s motivation in that text included the study of irreducibility, and specialization of Galois groups. Indeed, if $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ is an irreducible polynomial over $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , there is a thin set $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ such that for $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\not\in M$ , $F(Y,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , and there is a thin set $M^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ such that for $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\not\in M^{\prime}$ , $F(Y,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$ has the same Galois group as $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ over $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ [Ser97, §9.2-9.3].

Serre asked how many points of bounded height can lie in a thin set, and this question has motivated significant research since the 1980’s, culminating in a series of recent breakthroughs (including [Sal23] and [BCS+25]). The first goal of the present manuscript is to survey recent results, within the context of the four paradigms for thin sets, according to the projective/affine and type I/type II designations. Since some central questions within the four paradigms have recently been resolved completely, it is a good time to take stock, and also to highlight remaining open questions.

The second goal of the present manuscript is to consider questions of uniformity: how does an upper bound for the number of points in a thin set $M$ depend on the variety $X$ that characterizes the thin set? Famously, in the setting of type I thin sets, the best-known upper bound for the number of points of bounded height is independent of the maximum size, say $\|F\|$ , of the coefficients of the polynomials defining $X$ ; such an upper bound is called uniform. In the case of type II thin sets, no such uniform upper bound is known. We first recall an upper bound due to Serre [Ser97], with unspecified dependence on $\|F\|$ , which has served as a baseline for over 40 years. We refine the method of Serre to clarify how the implicit constant may depend on $\|F\|$ , in certain special cases. Then, we describe a different method to prove the baseline upper bound, first noted in our recent work [BPW25]; this method applies in full generality and shows there is at most polylogarithmic dependence on $\|F\|$ . Finally, we construct counterexamples to a specific type of strong, uniform upper bound for points in affine thin sets of type II, indicating that the question of uniformity may be more subtle for type II than for type I thin sets.

### 1.2. Thin sets of type I and type II: definitions

In order to survey recent progress in detail, we now define two types of thin set, which Serre distinguished in [Ser97, Ch. 9], and also in [Ser92, §3.1]. We state the definitions first in the projective setting:

Type I: A projective thin set $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ is of type I if there is a Zariski-closed subvariety $V\subsetneq\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ such that $M\subset V(\mathbb{Q})$ .

Type II: A projective thin set $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ is of type II if there is an irreducible projective algebraic variety $Z$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{P}}Z=\dim_{\mathbb{P}}(\mathbb{P}^{n-1})$ , and a dominant morphism $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ with generically finite fibres, of degree $d\geq 2$ , with $M\subset\pi(Z(\mathbb{Q}))$ .

Type I and type II affine thin sets $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ are defined in an analogous way, with $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ replaced in each instance by $\mathbb{A}^{n}$ , and projective replaced by affine. (Serre’s presentation of thin sets in [Ser97, Ch. 9, 13] is stated over any number field; we restrict our attention in the present survey to $\mathbb{Q}$ .) With an analytic number theory audience in mind, we provide a motivation for these two types, and prove the following lemma in §2.2-2.3.

#### Lemma 1.1.

Every thin set in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ (respectively in $\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ ) is a finite union of thin sets of type I and type II.

There is a useful polynomial interpretation of the type I/type II dichotomy, which we review in the affine setting, as in Serre [Ser97, §9.1]. If $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ is an affine thin set of type I, then there is a nonconstant polynomial $G\in\mathbb{Q}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ such that

$$ M\subset\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}:G(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=0\}. $$

On the other hand, given an irreducible $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})[Y]$ , a polynomial in $Y$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ , then the following set is an affine thin set of type II:

$$ \{\bfx\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}:\text{$\bfx$ not a pole of any coefficient of $F$, $F(Y,\bfx)=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Q}$}\}\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Q}). $$

By replacing $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ by a multiple $\tilde{F}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ of $F$ by an appropriate polynomial in $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ so that $\tilde{F}(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ , the set depicted above is contained in the set

$$ \{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}:\text{$\tilde{F}(Y,\mathbf{x})=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Q}$}\}. $$

Thus it is no loss of generality to assume that within (1.1), $F$ is a polynomial $Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ . Moreover, modulo a thin set of type I, every thin set of type II takes the form of (1.1), in the following sense (as we prove in §2.4, following [Ser97, Bro03a, BCS+25]):

#### Lemma 1.2.

Let $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ be an affine thin set of type II, with corresponding irreducible affine variety $Z$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}Z=n$ , and dominant morphism $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n}$ with generically finite fibres, of degree $d\geq 2$ , such that $M\subset\pi(Z(\mathbb{Q}))$ . Then there exists a proper closed subset $V\subsetneq Z$ with associated morphism $\pi_{V}:=\left.\pi\right|_{V}$ , and an irreducible polynomial $F\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ that is monic in $Y$ and has $\deg_{Y}F=d$ , such that

$$ M\subset\left(\pi_{V}(V)\cup\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}:\text{$F(Y,\mathbf{x})=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Q}$}\}\right). $$

Moreover, $\pi_{V}(V)$ is a thin set of type I in $\mathbb{A}^{n}$ .

We remark that the degree of $\pi_{V}$ is inexplicit; see Remark 2.7.

### 1.3. The counting problems

Our focus is on counting points of bounded height in a thin set, a suite of problems formulated explicitly by Serre [Ser97, §13]. In the projective setting, let $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ be a thin set, and for each $\mathbf{x}=[x_{1}:\ldots:x_{n}]\in\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ represented by $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ with $\gcd(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=1$ , define $\|\mathbf{x}\|=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_{i}|$ . Define the counting function

$$ N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(M,B):=\#\{\mathbf{x}\in M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q}):\gcd(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=1,\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq B\}. $$

Certainly $N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(M,B)\ll_{n}B^{n}$ is trivially true for all $B\geq 1$ .

In the affine setting, suppose $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ is a thin set, and for each integral point $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ define $\|\mathbf{x}\|=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_{i}|$ . Then define the counting function

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M,B):=\#\{\mathbf{x}\in M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z}):\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq B\}. $$

Certainly $N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M,B)\ll_{n}B^{n}$ is trivially true for all $B\geq 1$ .

The following nontrivial upper bound was established by Serre in [Ser97, Ch. 13 Thm. 1], and is closely related to work of Cohen [Coh81, Thm. 2.1].

#### Theorem 1.3 (Baseline upper bound).

For any thin set $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ , for some $C(M)\geq 1$ and $\gamma(M)>0$ ,

$$ N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(M,B)\leq C(M)B^{n-1/2}(\log(B+2))^{\gamma(M)},\qquad\text{for all $B\geq 1$.} $$

For any thin set $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ , for some $C(M)\geq 1$ and $\gamma(M)>0$ ,

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M,B)\leq C(M)B^{n-1/2}(\log(B+2))^{\gamma(M)},\qquad\text{for all $B\geq 1$.} $$

We will return momentarily to the dependence of $C(M)$ (and the exponent $\gamma(M)$ ) on $M$ , which is a significant focus of the present paper.

A basic observation is in order, following [Ser97, p. 187]; we provide a proof in §2.5.

#### Lemma 1.4.

Given a thin set $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ , define the set

$$ M^{\prime}=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}:p(\mathbf{x})\in M\}\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z}), $$

in which $p$ maps the tuple $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$ into $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ . Then $M^{\prime}$ is a thin set in $\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ and

$$ N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(M,B)\leq N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M^{\prime},B). $$

Moreover, if $M$ is of type I then $M^{\prime}$ is a finite union of thin sets of type I; if $M$ is type II then $M^{\prime}$ is a finite union of thin sets of type I and type II.

Thus to establish the baseline upper bound (1.4) for all projective thin sets, it suffices to prove the affine result (1.5). However, if one aims to improve on the baseline exponent $n-1/2$ in (1.4), this relationship is of limited use: on the one hand Serre observed that the affine bound (1.5) is essentially sharp (see Example 4.4). On the other hand, Serre asked an influential question about the projective setting:

#### Conjecture 1.5 (Thin set, projective).

For any thin set $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ , for some $C(M)\geq 1$ and $\gamma(M)>0$ ,

$$ N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(M,B)\leq C(M)B^{n-1}(\log(B+2))^{\gamma(M)}\qquad\text{for all $B\geq 1$.} $$

This prediction is stated in both [Ser97, p. 178 after Thm. 3] and [Ser92, p. 27]. Comparing this conjecture to the fact that (1.5) cannot be improved shows it is essential to consider the affine and projective settings separately—yet they also interact in important ways. In §3-§4, we present a survey of results on counting points in thin sets, which clearly separates out each of the four combinations of projective/affine and type I/type II designations. In particular, we remark that Conjecture 1.5 has now largely been resolved by the recent work of [BCS+25], with related progress in the affine case in work of the authors [BPW25].

### 1.4. Questions of dependence and uniformity

In the second half of the paper we present original results, focused on obtaining refined information for $C(M)$ and $\gamma(M)$ in Theorem 1.3, and with a specific focus on affine type II thin sets. Given any polynomial $F\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ , define

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B):=\#\{\bfx\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\text{ $F(Y,\bfx)=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$}\}. $$

It is always trivially true that $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\ll B^{n}$ (and this is sharp in the case that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ has $\deg_{Y}F\leq 1$ ). To prove Theorem 1.3 for an arbitrary affine thin set (and hence also for an arbitrary projective thin set, by (1.6)), it will suffice to prove for all polynomials $F$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ that are absolutely irreducible (that is, irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ ),

$$ N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)\leq C(F)B^{n-\frac{1}{2}}(\log(B+2))^{\gamma(F)}\qquad\text{for all $B\geq 1$,} $$

in which $C(F)$ and $\gamma(F)$ are positive constants that may depend on $F$ . (That this is sufficient is suggested already by Lemma 1.2, and we will provide the details in §4.) Let $\|F\|$ denote the maximum absolute value of any coefficient of $F$ . We say an upper bound of the form (1.9) is uniform if $C(F)$ (and $\gamma(F)$ ) depend at most on $n$ and the total degree of $F$ , but are independent of $\|F\|$ .

Serre’s original treatment proves (1.9) via the large sieve, for any absolutely irreducible polynomial $F$ , with a choice of $\gamma(F)<1$ but unspecified dependence of $C(F)$ on $\|F\|$ [Ser97, Ch. 13, Thm. 1]. In Theorem 5.1, we prove that in the special case that

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X}) Y^{m} m\geq 2 $$

Serre’s strategy can be refined to prove (1.9) with a constant $C(F)$ that exhibits at most polylogarithmic dependence on $\|F\|$ . For $m=1$ (so that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is only assumed to be monic in $Y$ ), we observe that this refinement can be obtained under the assumption of GRH for a single Dedekind zeta function. (We also remark that contemporaneous with Serre’s work, Cohen studied an upper bound for the number of specializations of a polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ to $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ for which the corresponding Galois group is not preserved [Coh81, Thm. 2.1]. Modifying Cohen’s approach yields an upper bound of the form (1.9) with $C(F)$ having at most polynomial dependence on $\|F\|$ (over an arbitrary number field). We consider Cohen’s strategy in detail in a different work [BPW26].)

In our recent work [BPW25] we require a stronger result, namely that (1.9) holds with $C(F)$ having at most polylogarithmic dependence on $\|F\|$ , without assuming the special structure (1.10) of $F$ . In Theorem 6.1 we prove such a bound; this argument originally appeared as [BPW25, Thm. 2.13]. This confirms that Theorem 1.3 holds, with $C(M)$ having at most polylog dependence on the coefficients of the polynomial(s) defining the thin set $M$ .

Finally, we consider the question of (potential) uniformity when bounding $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B)$ , in the setting of affine thin sets of type II. As we will survey in §3, the uniformity of estimates for $N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(M,B)$ and $N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M,B)$ has been extensively studied when $M$ is a thin set of type I. In §7 we raise the question of whether uniformity for thin sets of type II is more subtle. In particular, we present counterexamples to a (putative) uniform upper bound for affine thin sets of type II, and prove:

#### Theorem 1.6.

Let $n\geq 1$ be given. As $k$ varies over positive integers, there is a family of thin sets $M_{k}\in\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ of type II, defined by polynomials $F_{k}$ with $\|F_{k}\|=k$ , for which there is no constant $c>0$ such that

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M_{k},B)\ll_{n,\deg F_{k}}B^{n-1}(\log B)^{c} $$

can hold as $k\rightarrow\infty$ , with an implicit constant independent of $k$ .

### 1.5. Notation

We use $A\ll B$ to denote that $|A|\leq CB$ for some constant $C>0$ , where $B$ is non-negative. We use $A\ll_{\kappa}B$ to denote that the constant $C$ may depend upon the parameter $\kappa$ . We record the five main counting functions extensively studied in this paper.

- • $N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(M,B):=\#\{\mathbf{x}\in M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q}):\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n},\gcd(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=1,\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq B\},$ for a thin set $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ .

- • $N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M,B):=\#\{\mathbf{x}\in M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z}):\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n},\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq B\},$ for a thin set $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ .

- • $N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B):=\#\{\mathbf{x}\in V\cap\mathbb{P}^{N}(\mathbb{Q}):\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N+1})\in\mathbb{Z}^{N+1},\gcd(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N+1})=1,\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq B\}$ , for an irreducible projective variety $V\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}$ .

- • $N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V,B):=\#\{\mathbf{x}\in V\cap\mathbb{A}^{N}(\mathbb{Z}):\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N})\in\mathbb{Z}^{N},\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq B\},$ for an irreducible affine variety $V\subset\mathbb{A}^{N}$ .

- • $N^{\mathrm{cov}}_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(F,B):=\{\bfx\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\text{$F(Y,\bfx)=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$}\}$ , for a polynomial $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ , relevant to affine thin sets of type II.

We may generally assume $B\geq 3$ so that $\log B\gg 1$ .

## 2. Preliminaries: motivation for thin sets of type I and type II

In this section we prove Lemmas 1.1, 1.2, and 1.4. The underlying construction leading to the two types of thin sets is intrinsically geometric, and thus we also provide a brief motivation of these ideas, with analytic number theorists in mind. We consider here the projective setting, but analogous arguments motivate the affine setting.

### 2.1. Terminology

We start by recalling some terminology. We define a variety $X$ over a field $k$ to be a (reduced) scheme $X$ such that the structure morphism $X\rightarrow\text{Spec}(k)$ is separated and of finite type (see [Sta26, Section $29.15$ ] for the definition of morphism of finite type, and [Sta26, Section 26.21] for the definition of separated morphism). For varieties $X,Y$ , a morphism $\pi:X\rightarrow Y$ is said to be dominant if the image $\pi(X)$ is dense in $Y$ . A morphism is said to be generically finite if the generic fibre is finite. In the setting of thin sets, we now confirm the following useful fact:

#### Lemma 2.1.

If $X$ is an irreducible variety and a morphism $\pi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ is given, the morphism $\pi$ is of finite type (and locally of finite type).

#### Proof.

To record the relevant citations to verify this, consider in general two integral schemes $X,Y$ of finite type over $\mathbb{Q}$ (and consequently locally of finite type over $\mathbb{Q}$ ) and let $f:X\rightarrow Y$ be a morphism (in our case, $f=\pi$ and $Y=\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ ). In particular, since $X$ is locally of finite type over $\mathbb{Q}$ , then a morphism $f:X\rightarrow Y$ is locally of finite type, by Lemma 29.15.8 in [Sta26, Section 01T0]. By Dfn. 29.15.1 (ibid), to conclude that $f$ is of finite type, it suffices to show that in addition to being locally of finite type, $f$ is quasi-compact. (As in Dfn. 5.12.1 [Sta26, Definition 005A], a topological space $V$ is quasi-compact if every open covering of $V$ has a finite subcover. A continuous map $f:X\rightarrow Y$ is quasi-compact if the inverse image $f^{-1}(V)$ of every quasi-compact open $V\subset Y$ is quasi-compact.) Thus suppose $V\subset Y$ is quasi-compact, and consider for the given morphism $f:X\rightarrow Y$ the inverse image $f^{-1}(V)$ . Since $X$ is a noetherian scheme ( $X\rightarrow\text{Spec}(k)$ is of finite type and hence $X$ is noetherian [Sta26, Lemma $29.15.6$ ]), then $f$ is quasi-compact thanks to [Sta26, Lemma $28.5.8$ ]. ∎

### 2.2. The two types

Recall the definition: A subset $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ is thin if there is an algebraic variety $X$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ and a morphism $\pi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ with the properties

(i) $M\subset\pi(X(\mathbb{Q}))$ , and

(ii) the fibre of $\pi$ over the generic point is finite and $\pi$ has no rational section over $\mathbb{Q}$ . Let us see how this leads to the distinction between type I and type II thin sets, as defined in §1.2, and the proof of Lemma 1.1.

Let $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ be a thin set, with corresponding variety $X$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ and morphism $\pi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ . We furthermore assume $X$ is irreducible and reduced. (This is sufficient for studying the general case, after decomposing $X$ into irreducible components.) There are naturally two cases to consider:

(I) $\pi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ is not dominant;

(II) $\pi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ is dominant.

Case (I): In the first case, the image $\pi(X)$ is not dense in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ , that is to say the closure $\overline{\pi(X)}$ is a proper closed subset of $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ . Since $M\subset\pi(X(\mathbb{Q}))$ by property (i) of the definition, it follows that $M$ is contained within the rational points $V(\mathbb{Q})$ of a proper closed subvariety $V\subsetneq\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ . This leads to the notion of a thin set of type I.

The second case, when $\pi$ is dominant, is more subtle. (Indeed, Serre called thin sets of type II the “most interesting case of a thin set” [Ser97, p. 121].)

We now record two lemmas:

#### Lemma 2.2 ([Gro66, Corollary $13.1.6$ ]).

If $f:X\rightarrow Y$ is a dominant morphism that is locally of finite type, and $r=\dim X-\dim Y$ , then every irreducible component of every fibre $f^{-1}(y)$ has dimension at least $r$ . In particular, if $f$ has generically finite fibres, then $r=0$ .

#### Lemma 2.3.

Let $X,Y$ be irreducible varieties over a field $k$ , and consider a dominant morphism $f:X\rightarrow Y$ of finite type with generically finite fibres. Then $f$ has degree $1$ if and only if $f$ has a rational section over $k$ .

We defer for now the proof of Lemma 2.3, and see how it applies to the case (II).

Case (II): By Lemma 2.2, since $\pi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ is a dominant morphism of finite type with generically finite fibres, it follows that $\dim_{\mathbb{P}}X=\dim_{\mathbb{P}}\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ . Next, by Lemma 2.3, $\pi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ has degree 1 if and only if $\pi$ has a rational section over $\mathbb{Q}$ . By property (ii) in the definition of thin set, $\pi$ does not have a rational section over $\mathbb{Q}$ , and thus it must be that $\pi$ has degree at least 2. Thus case (II) leads directly to the notion of a thin set of type II.

In preparation for proving Lemma 2.3 it is useful to set some terminology. For varieties $X,Y$ , a rational map $\pi:X\dashrightarrow Y$ is a morphism defined on an open dense set in $X$ . (More precisely, it is an equivalence class of pairs $\langle U,\phi_{U}\rangle$ where $U$ is a non-empty open subset of $X$ and $\phi_{U}$ is a morphism from $U$ to $Y$ , and $\langle U,\phi_{U}\rangle$ is equivalent to $\langle V,\phi_{V}\rangle$ if $\phi_{U}$ and $\phi_{V}$ agree on $U\cap V$ ; see [Har77, Ch. I Section 4], from which the definitions in this discussion are taken.) A section of a morphism $f:X\rightarrow Y$ is a morphism $s:Y\rightarrow X$ such that $f\circ s$ is the identity morphism on $Y$ . A rational section $s$ of $f:X\rightarrow Y$ is a rational map $s:Y\dashrightarrow X$ such that $f\circ s=\mathrm{id}_{Y}$ , as a rational map (i.e. on an open dense subset of $Y$ ). To consider the notion of the degree of a morhpism $f$ , we recall another fact:

#### Lemma 2.4.

For varieties $X,Y$ over a field $k$ , a generically finite dominant morphism $f:X\rightarrow Y$ yields an induced map

$$ f^{*}:k(Y)\rightarrow k(X) $$

on the corresponding function fields, defined by pulling back rational functions from $Y$ to $X$ ; that is to say, acting by $f^{*}:r\mapsto r\circ f$ . The induced map $f^{*}$ is injective, under the hypothesis that $f$ is dominant.

#### Proof.

Suppose that a rational function $r\in k(Y)$ (defined on a dense open set $U_{Y}\subset Y$ ) lies in the kernel of $f^{*}$ , so that $r\circ f=0$ . Without loss of generality we may assume that $r=P/Q$ , for some $P,Q\in\mathbb{C}[\bfX]$ on $U_{Y}$ ; note also that since $U_{Y}$ is dense and open then its complement $Y\setminus U_{Y}$ is nowhere dense in $Y$ . Since $r(f(x))=0$ for every $x\in X$ such that $f(x)\in U_{Y}$ , it follows that upon defining $V:=U_{Y}\cap f(X)$ , the restriction $\left.r\right|_{V}=0=\left.P\right|_{V}$ . Now under the hypothesis that $f:X\rightarrow Y$ is dominant, the image $f(X)$ is dense in $Y$ , and this implies that the set $U_{Y}\cap f(X)$ is also dense in $Y$ . (For upon writing $f(X)=(U_{Y}\cap f(X))\cup((Y\setminus U_{Y})\cap f(X))$ , the fact that $((Y\setminus U_{Y})\cap f(X))$ is nowhere dense (as a subset of the nowhere dense set $Y\setminus U_{Y}$ ) forces $U_{Y}\cap f(X)$ to be dense.) Hence $P$ is zero on the dense set $U_{Y}\cap f(X)$ in $Y$ , so it must be the zero polynomial, and consequently $\left.P\right|_{U_{Y}}=0$ . This implies $\left.r\right|_{U_{Y}}=0$ on the dense open set $U_{Y}$ , so $r$ lies in the same equivalence class as the zero map on $Y$ ; that is, we may say $r=0$ (see Dfn. 29.49.1 in [Sta26, Section 01RR]). Thus $f^{*}$ is injective, as claimed. ∎

With the knowledge that the induced map is injective, the degree of $f$ is then defined to be

$$ \deg f:=[k(X):f^{*}k(Y)], $$

the degree of the function field $k(X)$ as a (finite) extension of fields of $f^{*}k(Y)$ . Notice that the fact that $f$ is a dominant, generically finite, morphism of finite type and $X,Y$ are integral schemes guarantees that $\deg f<\infty$ . Indeed, since $f:X\rightarrow Y$ is generically finite, we can find two affine open subsets $U\subset X$ , and $V\subset Y$ such that $\left.f\right|_{U}:U\rightarrow V$ is finite. Since $f_{|U}$ is finite and dominant ( $U$ and $V$ are dense in $X$ and $Y$ respectively and $X,Y$ are irreducible), we have that $[k(U):k(V)]<\infty$ . On the other hand since $U,V$ are dense in the integral schemes $X,Y$ , one has $k(U)=k(X)$ , and $k(V)=k(Y).$ See [Har77, Chapter II Exercise 3.7], and also Dfn. 29.51.8 in [Sta26, Section 02NV].

Next, we consider in particular the case of degree 1:

#### Lemma 2.5.

Under the hypotheses of Lemma 2.4, $f:X\rightarrow Y$ has degree 1 if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are birationally equivalent.

To parse this, recall that a birational map $\phi:X\dashrightarrow Y$ is a rational map with an inverse $\psi:Y\dashrightarrow X$ such that $\psi\circ\phi=\mathrm{id}_{X}$ as a rational map, and $\phi\circ\psi=\mathrm{id}_{Y}$ as a rational map. If such a birational map exists, $X$ and $Y$ are said to be birationally equivalent.

#### Proof.

By definition, $f$ has degree 1 precisely when $[k(X):f^{*}k(Y)]=1$ , so that (equivalently) the induced map $f^{*}:k(Y)\rightarrow k(X)$ is not only injective but also surjective; that is to say, the function fields $k(X)$ and $k(Y)$ are isomorphic, with isomorphism $f^{*}$ . It is a classical result that $k(X)$ and $k(Y)$ are isomorphic precisely when $X$ and $Y$ are birationally equivalent [Har77, Ch. I Cor. 4.5] (see also [Sta26, Ch. 29 Dfn. 49.11] and subsequent remark). ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 2.3.

Now to prove Lemma 2.3, suppose that a dominant morphism $f:X\rightarrow Y$ of finite type with generically finite fibre has degree 1, so that by the discussion above, $X$ and $Y$ are birationally equivalent, with isomorphism $f^{*}:k(Y)\rightarrow k(X)$ . After passing to an affine cover for $X$ and $Y$ , we may proceed in the case that $X$ and $Y$ are affine. Then by [Har77, Ch. I Prop. 3.5] there is a bijection between $\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)$ and $\mathrm{Hom}(A(Y),A(X))$ (in which $A(X)$ denotes the coordinate ring, with $k(X)$ isomorphic to the quotient field of $A(X)$ , and analogously for $Y$ [Har77, Ch. I Thm. 3.2]). Thus there exists a morphism $g:Y\rightarrow X$ such that $g^{*}=(f^{*})^{-1}$ . Now take $f\circ g$ ; then since $(f\circ g)^{*}=g^{*}\circ f^{*}=\Id_{k(Y)}$ , then by a second application of [Har77, Ch. I Prop. 3.5], we conclude that $f\circ g=\Id_{Y}$ . Since a morphism is a rational map (defined on $Y$ itself), this suffices to show $f$ has a rational section.

In the other direction, suppose that a dominant morphism $f:X\rightarrow Y$ has a rational section, so that there is a rational map $s:Y\dashrightarrow X$ (defined on a dense open subset $U_{Y}$ of $Y$ ) such that $f\circ s=\mathrm{id}_{Y}$ as a rational map. Then by [Har77, Ch. I Prop. 3.5],

$$ (f\circ s)^{*}=s^{*}\circ f^{*}=\mathrm{Id}_{k(Y)}. $$

Since $f^{*}:k(Y)\rightarrow k(X)$ and $s^{*}:k(X)\rightarrow k(Y)$ , the property (2.2) can only be achieved if $s^{*}$ is surjective. A ring homomorphism acting on a field (here $k(X)$ ) is either injective or the zero map, and since $s^{*}$ is surjective it is not the zero map, so $s^{*}$ is injective as well, and hence provides an isomorphism so that $k(X)\cong k(Y)$ . Hence $\deg[k(X):k(Y)]=1$ , and finally this implies $\deg f=1$ , as desired. ∎

We close this section with a few final remarks. Recall the notation of §1.2. For clarity, let us confirm that a set that satisfies the condition of being type I is a thin set: one may take $X=V$ and $\pi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ to be the inclusion map, for which the generic fibre is empty since $V$ is a proper closed subset. Similarly, let us confirm that a set of type II is a thin set: one may take $X=Z$ and $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ the dominant morphism with generically finite fibres; recall that by hypothesis $\dim_{\mathbb{P}}Z=\dim_{\mathbb{P}}(\mathbb{P}^{n-1})$ . Since $\deg(\pi)\geq 2$ , $\pi$ has no rational section over $\mathbb{Q}$ , by Lemma 2.3. Finally, the space of thin sets is closed under finite union, that is, any finite union of thin sets is thin.

### 2.3. Proof of Lemma 1.1

Given a thin set $M$ with corresponding variety $X$ and morphism $\pi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ such that $M\subset\pi(X(\mathbb{Q}))$ , decompose $X=\cup_{i=1}^{m}V_{i}$ into irreducible components. Then for every $i=1,...,m$ we have a morphism $\pi_{i}=\left.\pi\right|_{V_{i}}:V_{i}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ , and upon setting $M_{i}=M\cap\pi_{i}(V_{i}(\mathbb{Q}))$ then $M=\cup_{i=1}^{n}M_{i}$ . The discussion in §2.2 shows that if $\left.\pi\right|_{V_{i}}$ is dominant then $M_{i}$ is a thin set of type II, while if not, then $M_{i}$ is a thin set of type I. This completes the proof of Lemma 1.1.

### 2.4. Proof of Lemma 1.2

To prove the lemma, we adapt portions from the proof of [Bro03a, Lemma 3], following a remark of Serre [Ser97, p. 122]; see also Proposition 4.5, which is due to [BCS+25]. Define $U\subset Z$ to be the affine variety $\pi^{-1}(\mathbb{A}^{n})$ , and let $k(U)$ denote the function field of $U$ . (Note for later reference that $Z\setminus U$ is a proper closed subset of $Z$ . Certainly $Z\setminus U$ is a proper subset of $Z$ , since otherwise $U$ would be empty, contradicting the fact that $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n}$ is dominant. Additionally, $Z\setminus U$ is closed in $Z$ , since the pre-image $U$ of the open set $\mathbb{A}^{n}$ is open, under the morphism $\pi$ .) Let $t$ be a generator of $k(U)$ over $k(\mathbb{A}^{n})=\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , chosen so that its minimal polynomial, say

$$ F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})=Y^{d}+f_{1}(\mathbf{X})Y^{d-1}+\cdots+f_{d}(\mathbf{X}), $$

has coefficients $f_{j}(\mathbf{X})$ that are polynomials with integral coefficients. Now consider the affine variety $W\subset\mathbb{A}^{n+1}$ defined by $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=0$ , as well as the projection map $p:W\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n}$ given by $p(Y,\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}$ . By construction, the function fields $k(U)$ and $k(W)$ are isomorphic (indeed, they are both isomorphic to $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})(t)$ ). Consequently, by Lemma 2.5, $U$ and $W$ are birationally equivalent, and in particular there is a (bi)rational map $r:U\dashrightarrow W$ , with an accompanying (bi)rational map $s:W\dashrightarrow U$ such that $s\circ r=\mathrm{id}_{U}$ and $r\circ s=\mathrm{id}_{W}$ (in each case, as a rational map, that is, on an open dense subset).

From this, observe that there is a proper closed subset $U_{0}\subset U$ such that

$$ \pi^{\prime}:=\left.\pi\right|_{U\setminus U_{0}}:U\setminus U_{0}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n} $$

factors through $p:W\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n}$ . Indeed, by the existence of the birational map $r:U\dashrightarrow W$ there is some open dense subset of $U$ upon which $r$ is a morphism; we define $U_{0}$ to be the complement of that subset. Then $\pi^{\prime}:=\left.\pi\right|_{U\setminus U_{0}}=p\circ r$ , as in the following diagram:

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U\setminus U_{0}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{A}^{n}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi^{\prime}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p} $$

Finally, define $V\subset Z$ by $V=U_{0}\cup(Z\setminus U)$ . First note that $V$ is a proper closed subset of $Z$ , since as observed earlier, each of $U_{0}$ and $Z\setminus U$ is a proper closed subset of $Z$ . Second, by arguing as above, note that $\pi^{\prime\prime}:=\left.\pi\right|_{Z\setminus V}:Z\setminus V\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n}$ factors through $p:W\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n}$ . That is to say, on $Z\setminus V$ , $\pi^{\prime\prime}=p\circ s$ for some morphism $s:Z\setminus V\rightarrow W$ .

By applying $\pi$ to $Z=V\cup(Z\setminus V)$ , we then see that

$$ \pi(Z)\subset(\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V)\cup\left.\pi\right|_{Z\setminus V}(Z\setminus V))\\
=(\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V)\cup(p\circ s)(Z\setminus V))\subset(\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V)\cup p(W))). $$

In particular,

$$ M\subset\pi(Z(\mathbb{Q}))\subset(\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V(\mathbb{Q}))\cup\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}:\text{$F(Y,\mathbf{x})=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Q}$}\}). $$

The last step is to verify:

#### Lemma 2.6.

If $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n}$ is a dominant morphism with generically finite fibres of degree $d\geq 2$ and $V\subsetneq Z$ is a proper closed subset, then $\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V)$ is a thin set of type I in $\mathbb{A}^{n}$ .

#### Proof.

It suffices to show $\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V)$ is contained in a proper closed subset of $\mathbb{A}^{n}$ , which we will do in two steps. First we will confirm that $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V)\leq n-1$ in $\mathbb{A}^{n}$ . Second, any set $W\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ with dimension $<n$ is contained in a proper closed subset.

For the first step, we note that there exists an open subset $U\subset V$ on which $\left.\pi\right|_{V}$ is finite, since $\pi$ has generically finite fibers. As $\left.\pi\right|_{U}$ is finite, by Lemma 2.2 we see $\left.\pi\right|_{U}(U)=\dim_{\mathbb{A}}U=\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V\leq n-1$ . Additionally, $\left.\pi\right|_{U}(U)$ is an open subset of $\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V)$ (with respect to the topology on $\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V)$ ), so $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}\left.\pi\right|_{U}(U)=\dim_{\mathbb{A}}\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V)\leq n-1$ .

For the second step, let us verify that if $W\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ has $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}W<n$ , then $W$ is contained in a proper closed subset of $\mathbb{A}^{n}$ . For suppose on the contrary that $W$ is not contained in any proper closed subset. Then for every (nonempty) open set $U\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ , $W\not\subset U^{c}$ , so $W\cap U$ is nonempty. Thus $W$ is dense in $\mathbb{A}^{n}$ , so that $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}W=\dim_{\mathbb{A}}\overline{W}=\dim_{\mathbb{A}}\mathbb{A}^{n}$ , a contradiction. ∎

#### Remark 2.7 (Inexplicit aspect of Lemma 1.2).

Lemma 2.6 confirms that $\left.\pi\right|_{V}(V)$ is a thin set of type I in $\mathbb{A}^{n}$ , but it provides no bound on the degree of this thin set. This inexplicitness presents a barrier to obtaining a uniform upper bound when counting integral points in the thin set of type II considered in Lemma 1.2, a subject considered extensively later in the paper.

### 2.5. Proof of Lemma 1.4: simple relation between projective and affine thin sets

Let $M$ be the given thin set in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ . Since $M$ is a finite union of type I and type II thin sets in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ , it suffices to consider those cases individually.

#### 2.5.1. Type I

Suppose $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ is of type I, so that for some Zariski-closed (irreducible) variety $V\subsetneq\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ , $M\subset V(\mathbb{Q})$ . Denote homogeneous coordinates in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ by $[x_{1}:\cdots:x_{n}]$ . For each $i$ let $U_{i}$ be the open subset $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}\setminus\{x_{i}=0\}$ . Then for each $i$ , $U_{i}$ can be identified with $\mathbb{A}^{n-1}$ by

$$ [x_{1}:\cdots:x_{i}:\cdots:x_{n}]\mapsto(x_{1}/x_{i},\ldots,x_{n}/x_{i}), $$

omitting the $i$ th place in the image. Then $V_{i}:=V\cap U_{i}$ is an open subset of $V$ and can be identified with an affine variety $\widetilde{V}_{i}\subset\mathbb{A}^{n-1}$ (which has $V$ as its projective closure). This affine variety is closed, and is irreducible since its projective closure $V$ is irreducible (see [Sha13, §4.5 Ex. 1] or [Rei88, §5.5 Prop.]).

On the other hand, $\mathbb{A}^{n}\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$ can be written as a union $\cup_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}$ in which $A_{i}=\mathbb{A}^{n}\setminus\{x_{i}=0\}$ . Each set $A_{i}$ can be identified with $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ by

$$ p_{i}:(x_{1},\ldots,x_{i},\ldots,x_{n})\mapsto[x_{1}:\cdots:x_{i}:\cdots:x_{n}]=[x_{1}/x_{i}:\cdots:1:\cdots:x_{n}/x_{i}]. $$

In the definition of $M^{\prime}$ in the lemma, we will regard the map $p(\mathbf{x})$ as acting by $p_{i}(\mathbf{x})$ for $\mathbf{x}\in A_{i}$ . For $M^{\prime}$ as in the lemma, write $M^{\prime}=\cup_{i=1}^{n}M_{i}^{\prime}$ with $M_{i}=M^{\prime}\cap A_{i}$ . Then for any $\mathbf{x}\in M_{i}^{\prime}$ , $p(\mathbf{x})\in U_{i}$ and $p(\mathbf{x})\in M\subset V$ , so that $p(\mathbf{x})\in V_{i}=V\cap U_{i}$ . Consequently, $M_{i}^{\prime}\subset\widetilde{V}_{i}(\mathbb{Z})\subset\mathbb{A}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Z})\subsetneq\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ . Thus $M_{i}^{\prime}$ is a thin set of type I. In conclusion $M^{\prime}$ is a finite union of thin sets of type I.

#### 2.5.2. Type II

Next, suppose $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ is of type II, so there is an irreducible projective algebraic variety $Z\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{P}}Z=\dim_{\mathbb{P}}(\mathbb{P}^{n-1})$ , and a dominant morphism $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ with generically finite fibres, of degree $d\geq 2$ , with $M\subset\pi(Z(\mathbb{Q}))$ . Similar to the argument above, define for each $j=1,\ldots,N$ the affine cover $Z_{j}=Z\cap U_{j}$ for $U_{j}=\mathbb{P}^{N}\setminus\{x_{j}=0\}$ ; then $Z_{j}$ is an open dense subset of $Z$ . Consider the morphism $\pi_{j}:Z_{j}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ defined by $\pi_{j}=\left.\pi\right|_{Z_{j}}$ . As in the discussion of §2.2, there are two cases: if $\pi_{j}$ is not dominant, then $\pi_{j}(Z_{j})$ is a thin set of type I, so the previous case applies.

On the other hand, if $\pi_{j}$ is dominant, we claim $\pi_{j}(Z_{j})$ is a thin set of type II. This last observation merely requires checking that $\pi_{j}$ has degree at least 2. By Lemma 2.3, it suffices to show that if $\pi_{j}$ has a rational section then $\pi$ has a rational section. Suppose $\pi_{j}$ has a rational section, say a rational map $s:\mathbb{P}^{n-1}\dashrightarrow Z_{j}$ defined on a dense open set $O\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ such that $\pi_{j}\circ s=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}$ as a rational map, or in other words $\pi_{j}\circ s-\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}$ is the zero map, as a rational map. Since $Z_{j}$ is open and dense in $Z$ , arguing as in the proof of Lemma 2.4 shows that $\pi\circ s=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}$ . Thus $s$ is a rational section of $\pi$ , and the claim is verified.

Finally, define for each $j=1,\ldots,N$ , and $i=1,\ldots,n$ ,

$$ M^{\prime}_{i,j}=\{\mathbf{x}\in A_{i}:p(\mathbf{x})\in\pi_{j}(Z_{j}(\mathbb{Q}))\}. $$

Then for the affine set $M^{\prime}$ as defined in the lemma,

$$ M^{\prime}\subset\bigcup_{i,j}M^{\prime}_{i,j}. $$

Each set $M_{i,j}^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ is a thin set of type I or type II, so that $M^{\prime}$ is a union of thin sets, and hence is a thin set, and the lemma is proved.

#### Remark 2.8.

The elementary ideas of Lemma 1.4 can be compared to Proposition 3.12, which is a method for passing from a projective thin set of type I to a particular kind of affine thin set of type I, and to Proposition 4.5, which is a method of passing from a projective thin set of type II to the union of a particular kind of affine thin set of type II, and a thin set of type I.

## 3. Survey of type I thin sets and Dimension Growth

In this section we survey results on counting points in thin sets of type I.

### 3.1. Type I, projective

Consider a thin set $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ of type I in the projective setting. Let $V$ be a Zariski-closed subvariety $V\subsetneq\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ such that $M\subset V(\mathbb{Q})$ , so that

$$ N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(M,B)\leq\#\{\mathbf{x}\in V(\mathbb{Q}):\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n},\gcd(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=1,\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq B\}. $$

Thus in the type I setting, the central aim is to bound, for any irreducible projective variety $V\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}$ ,

$$ N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B):=\#\{\mathbf{x}\in V\cap\mathbb{P}^{N}(\mathbb{Q}):\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n},\gcd(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N+1})=1,\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq B\}. $$

We record a trivial bound:

#### Lemma 3.1 (Trivial bound, projective variety).

Given a projective variety $V\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}$ , then

$$ N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B)\ll_{\deg V,\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V,N}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V+1}. $$

This is best possible if $V$ is of degree 1. It is simple to show a non-uniform bound $N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B)\ll_{V}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V+1}$ . Indeed, upon letting $m=\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V$ , this bound follows from choosing homogeneous coordinates for $\mathbb{P}^{N}$ so that projection onto the first $m+1$ coordinates induces a finite morphism $\pi:V\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{m}.$ Each fibre of $\pi$ has a finite number of points (controlled by the degree of $\pi$ ), and then it suffices to count trivially the points in $\mathbb{P}^{m}$ of height at most $B$ ; see remarks following [Ser97, Ch. 13, Thm. 2]. A different, but still elementary, argument leads to the uniform bound in Lemma 3.1. It relies on a trivial bound in the affine setting (Lemma 3.9, proved independently in a section on affine results).

#### Proof.

Arguing as in the proof of Lemma 1.4 in §2.5 (or as in [Har77, Ch. I Cor 2.3]), for $V\subsetneq\mathbb{P}^{N}$ of projective dimension $m$ , we can define an affine variety

$$ V^{\prime}=\{\mathbf{x}:p(\mathbf{x})\in V\}\subset\mathbb{A}^{N+1}, $$

with $V^{\prime}=\cup_{i}V_{i}^{\prime}=\cup_{i}(V^{\prime}\cap A_{i})$ , in which $A_{i}=\mathbb{A}^{N+1}\setminus\{x_{i}=0\}$ for $i=1,\ldots,N+1$ . Decompose $N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B)\leq\sum_{i}N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V_{i}^{\prime},B)$ . Each $V_{i}^{\prime}$ has affine dimension $\leq m+1$ . A trivial bound in the affine setting then shows that $N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V_{i}^{\prime},B)\ll_{\deg V_{i}^{\prime},\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V_{i}^{\prime},N}B^{m+1}$ (see Lemma 3.9). This suffices for Lemma 3.1. ∎

#### Remark 3.2.

In particular, if $V$ is of pure dimension then the dependence in this lemma is at most linear in $\deg V$ , following Lemma 3.9. Dehennin has recently conjectured that the dependence on degree in this projective setting should be at most sublinear [Deh26, Conj. 1.3].

In the setting of (3.1), $V\subsetneq\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ has $\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V\leq n-2$ , and Lemma 3.1 implies

$$ N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(M,B)\leq N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B)\ll_{\deg V,n}B^{n-1}. $$

Thus certainly Conjecture 1.5 is met for projective thin sets of type I. Instead, in this case the relevant deep question is:

#### Conjecture 3.3 (Dimension Growth Conjecture, projective).

For any irreducible projective variety $V\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}$ of degree $d\geq 2$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ ,

$$ N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B)\leq C(V)B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V}s(B),\qquad\text{for all $B\geq 1$,} $$

in which $C(V)$ is a constant possibly depending on $V$ , and $s(B)$ is a “small factor,” which could take the form $s(B)\ll_{\varepsilon}B^{\varepsilon}$ (for any $\varepsilon>0$ ); or $s(B)\leq(\log B)^{\gamma(V)}$ for some $\gamma(V)>0$ ; or $s(B)\leq 1$ .

The main exponent is essentially the best that could be expected. For suppose that $V$ contains a rational linear subspace $V^{\prime}$ of codimension $1$ in $V$ ; then

$$ N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B)\geq N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V^{\prime},B)\gg B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V^{\prime}+1}=B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V}. $$

Serre provides an example for which a logarithmic small factor necessarily arises in (3.3) [Ser97, p. 178], as follows:

#### Example 3.4.

Consider the quadric $X_{1}X_{2}=X_{3}X_{4}$ in $\mathbb{P}^{3}$ . Denoting the divisor function $d(\cdot)$ ,

$$ N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B)\gg\sum_{z\leq B^{2}}d(z)\gg B^{2}\log B. $$

A refined conjecture asks for uniformity:

#### Conjecture 3.5 (Uniform Dimension Growth Conjecture, projective).

The Dimension Growth Conjecture 3.3 holds with a choice of $C(V)$ (and $\gamma(V)$ , if relevant) dependent on the degree and dimension of $V$ but not otherwise on $V$ .

Within the Uniform Dimension Growth Conjecture 3.5, it is also interesting to ask for explicit expressions for $C(V)$ (and $\gamma(V)$ , if relevant), in terms of the degree and dimension of $V$ .

Conjecture 3.3 was stated by Serre [Ser97, p. 178 after Thm. 4] and Heath-Brown, with a statement for (absolutely irreducible) hypersurfaces in [HB83, p. 227] and both non-uniform and uniform versions for hypersurfaces in [HB02, Conj. 1, Conj. 2]; see also a uniform version for varieties of any codimension in [BHBS06, Conj. 2]. By (3.1), Conjectures 3.3 and 3.5 would imply $N_{\mathbb{P}^{n-1}}(M,B)\leq C(V)B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V}s(B)$ for any projective thin set $M\subset V(\mathbb{Q})$ of type I of degree $d\geq 2$ .

We turn our attention to surveying works that recently resolved the Dimension Growth Conjecture 3.3, as well as the Uniform Dimension Growth Conjecture 3.5, in all but one case.

To prove Conjectures 3.3 and 3.5 we may restrict attention to varieties defined as the zero locus of forms that are all defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ , as remarked in [BHBS06, p.546]:

#### Lemma 3.6.

Let $V\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}$ be a projective variety, or let $V\subset\mathbb{A}^{N}$ be an affine variety, defined over a finite extension $k/\mathbb{Q}$ . If the ideal of $V$ is not invariant under the action of the absolute Galois group $\Gal(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ , then there exists a codimension 1 subvariety $Y\subset V$ with $\deg Y\ll_{k,N,\deg V}1$ such that $V(\mathbb{Q})\subseteq Y(\mathbb{Q})$ .

Consequently, by working within each irreducible component $V_{j}$ of $V$ to which the lemma applies, $V_{j}(\mathbb{Q})\subseteq Y_{j}(\mathbb{Q})$ for some codimension 1 subvariety $Y_{j}\subset V_{j}$ , with $\deg Y_{j}\ll_{k,N,\deg V_{j}}1$ . Then the trivial bound $N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V_{j},B)\ll_{\deg Y_{j},\dim_{\mathbb{P}}Y_{j},N}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}Y_{j}+1}\ll B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V_{j}}$ of Lemma 3.1 suffices to obtain Conjectures 3.3 and 3.5 in this case. (Here we note that the trivial bound in Lemma 3.1 applies regardless of the field of definition of the variety.)

#### Proof.

Let $I(V)$ denote the ideal of $V$ . Since $I(V)$ is not invariant under the action of $\Gal(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ , there exists an extension $k/\mathbb{Q}$ and a polynomial $f\in I(V)\subset k[\mathbf{X}]$ such that $g(f)\not\in I(V)$ for some $g\in\Gal(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ . Let $k=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ and $[k:\mathbb{Q}]=d$ ; then we can decompose $f$ in the following way:

$$ f(\mathbf{X})=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}f_{i}(\mathbf{X})\alpha^{i}, $$

where $f_{i}(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Q}[\mathbf{X}]$ for each $i,$ and $\deg f_{i}\ll_{k,N,\deg V}1$ . For $\mathbf{x}\in V(\mathbb{Q})$ , we must have that $f_{i}(\mathbf{x})=0$ for each $i.$ Thus, to show that $V(\mathbb{Q})$ lies in a proper subvariety, it suffices to show that $f_{i}(\mathbf{X})\not\in I(V)$ for some $i$ . This follows from the fact that

$$ (g(f))(\mathbf{X})=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}f_{i}(\mathbf{X})\cdot(g(\alpha^{i})); $$

if $f_{i}(\mathbf{X})\in I(V)$ for each $i$ , then $g(f)\in I(V)$ , a contradiction. Thus $f_{i}(\mathbf{X})\not\in I(V)$ for some $i$ but must vanish on all of $V(\mathbb{Q})$ , as desired.

∎

To prove Conjectures 3.3 and 3.5, it also suffices to consider only the case of geometrically integral varieties. Indeed:

#### Lemma 3.7.

Let $V\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}$ be a projective variety, or let $V\subset\mathbb{A}^{N}$ be an affine variety, defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ , of degree $d$ . If $V$ is integral but not geometrically integral, then there exists a codimension 1 subvariety $Y\subset V$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ of degree at most $d^{2}$ such that $V(\mathbb{Q})\subseteq Y(\mathbb{Q})$ .

Consequently if $V\subsetneq\mathbb{P}^{N}$ is integral but not geometrically integral then by Lemma 3.1,

$$ N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B)\ll_{\deg Y,\dim_{\mathbb{P}}Y,N}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}Y+1}=B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V}, $$

which suffices. We state the lemma as in [Ver24, Prop. 2.1], which cites the first paragraph of [Wal15, §4] for a proof of a similar result; see also [HB02, Cor. 1] and [Sal23, p. 1093] for analogous strategies. For completeness we record a proof.

#### Proof.

Assume $V$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ but not over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ one can write

$$ V=\bigcup_{i=1}^{\ell}W_{i}, $$

where for every $i=1,\ldots,\ell$ , the variety $W_{i}$ is irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and $W_{i}$ is not defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ . (Note that necessarily $\ell\geq 2$ , since if $\ell=1$ , then $W_{1}$ would be defined over the rationals, since $V$ is, yielding a contradiction.)

Moreover notice that $\deg W_{i}\leq d$ for every $i=1,\ldots,\ell$ . For each $i$ let $K_{i}/\mathbb{Q}$ be the minimal extension such that $W_{i}$ is defined over $K_{i}$ and let $\sigma_{i}\in\Gal(K_{i}/\mathbb{Q})$ be such that $\sigma_{i}(W_{i})\neq W_{i}$ . (Such a map exists since $W_{i}$ is not defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ , and also $\deg\sigma_{i}(W_{i})\leq d$ .) Then if $P\in\mathbb{Q}^{N}$ is a rational point we have that

$$ P\in W_{i}(\mathbb{Q})\Longleftrightarrow P\in\sigma_{i}(W_{i})(\mathbb{Q}). $$

Hence,

$$ \begin{split}P\in V(\mathbb{Q})&\Longrightarrow P\in W_{i}(\mathbb{Q})\text{ for some }i\in\{1,\cdots,\ell\}\\
&\Longrightarrow P\in(W_{i}\cap\sigma_{i}(W_{i}))(\mathbb{Q})\text{ for some }i\in\{1,\cdots,\ell\}.\end{split} $$

Thus

$$ V(\mathbb{Q})\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^{\ell}(W_{i}\cap\sigma_{i}(W_{i}))(\mathbb{Q}). $$

On the other hand, since $W_{i}$ is absolutely irreducible, it follows that $W_{i}\cap\sigma_{i}(W_{i})$ has codimension (at least) 1 in $W_{i}$ . Finally, since both $\deg(W_{i})\leq d$ and $\deg(\sigma_{i}(W_{i}))\leq d$ , then $\deg(W_{i}\cap\sigma_{i}(W_{i}))\leq d^{2}$ by Bézout’s Theorem [EH16, Cor. 2.4]. ∎

One of the most natural settings for studying the Dimension Growth Conjecture 3.3 is for $V\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ a nonsingular projective hypersurface of degree $d\geq 2$ . This case was resolved by combined works of Browning and Heath-Brown for all $n\geq 3$ [HB94, HB02, Bro03b, BHB06a, BHB06b]. In the general setting of a variety, one of the earliest results is due to Serre:

$$ N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B)\leq C(V)B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V+1/2}(\log B)^{\gamma(V)} $$

for some $\gamma(V)<1$ . (Serre deduced this in [Ser97, p. 178 Thms. 3,4] from an upper bound for projective thin sets of type II, which is in turn deduced from studying affine thin sets of type II via (1.6); we defer further discussion to Remark 4.2.) To make further progress, Browning, Heath-Brown, and Salberger showed that a bound for $N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B)$ can be obtained from a bound for a corresponding affine problem for hypersurfaces [BHBS06, Thm. 1]. That is, controlling projective thin sets of type I can be achieved by controlling certain affine thin sets of type I, so we now turn our attention to that case.

### 3.2. Type I, affine

Consider $M\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ a thin set of type I. Let $V$ be a Zariski-closed subvariety $V\subsetneq\mathbb{A}^{n}$ such that $M\subset V(\mathbb{Z})$ . Since

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M,B)\leq\#\{\mathbf{x}\in V\cap\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z}):\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq B\}, $$

improving on the trivial bound reduces to a question about counting integral points of bounded height on an irreducible affine variety. Given any irreducible affine variety $V\subset\mathbb{A}^{N}$ , define

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V,B):=\#\{\mathbf{x}\in V\cap\mathbb{A}^{N}(\mathbb{Z}):\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq B\}. $$

In the special case that $V$ is a hypersurface $H$ defined as the vanishing set of a polynomial $F(X_{1},\ldots,X_{N})\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{N}]$ , the trivial bound is also sometimes called the Schwartz-Zippel bound:

#### Lemma 3.8 (Trivial bound, affine hypersurface).

Let $A$ be a domain, such as $\mathbb{Z}$ , or $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ for a prime $p$ , or the ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_{k}$ in a number field $k$ . Let $F\in A[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be a nonzero polynomial of degree $d\geq 1$ , and $S\subset A$ a finite subset. Then

$$ \#\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in S^{n}:F(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=0\}\leq d|S|^{n-1}. $$

The proof is by induction on dimension, and may be found in many places, such as [HB02, Thm. 1] or [BCLP23, Lemma 10.1]. (While the proof given in [HB02, Thm. 1] is stated in the setting where $F$ is absolutely irreducible, and the proof given in [BCLP23, Lemma 10.1] is stated in the case where $F$ is homogeneous, either proof applies in the present setting via trivial modifications.)

In the general where $V$ is a variety, a trivial bound is:

#### Lemma 3.9 (Trivial bound, affine variety).

For any variety $V\subsetneq\mathbb{A}^{N}$ ,

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V,B)\ll_{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V,\deg V,N}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V}. $$

If moreover $V$ is of pure dimension, the dependence can be made explicit as

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V,B)\ll_{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V,N}(\deg V)B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V}. $$

The exponent is best possible if $V$ is of degree 1. In general if $V\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ is an affine variety, a nonuniform bound $N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V,B)\ll_{V}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V}$ can again be obtained by an argument that projects from $\mathbb{A}^{N}$ to $\mathbb{A}^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V}$ , analogous to the remark following Lemma 3.1. For completeness, we now provide a proof of the uniform version recorded in the present lemma. This proof is similar to [BHB05, Thm. 1], and the result stated above can also be found for example in [CCDN20, Lemma 4.1.1], [BCS+25, Prop. 2.1]. It is an interesting feature that the constant in the affine Schwartz-Zippel bound in Lemma 3.8 and Lemma 3.9 has linear dependence on $\deg V$ . (If $V$ is a union of $d$ parallel linear varieties, this dependence on $d=\deg V$ cannot be improved.) In contrast, see Remark 3.2.

#### Proof.

For clarity, we suppose the given variety $V$ is defined over a field $k$ . In this paper we only require the case $k=\mathbb{Q}$ , or a number field $k$ in the application following Lemma 3.6 via Lemma 3.1. Thus we assume here for simplicity that $k$ is a number field, although the proof can be adapted to more general settings, since it only relies on Lemma 3.8.

Decompose $V$ into irreducible components (over $k$ ) as $V=\cup_{j\in J}W_{j}$ , in which there are at most $\deg V$ components. Consequently, to prove the main claim of the lemma, it is sufficient to prove that for any irreducible variety $W\subset\mathbb{A}^{N}$ defined over $k$ ,

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(W,B)\ll_{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}W,N}(\deg W)B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}W}. $$

Applying this to each irreducible component in $V$ leads to

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V,B)\ll_{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V,N}(\sum_{j\in J}\deg W_{j})B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V}. $$

Recall that the degree of $V$ is the sum of the degrees of the irreducible components of $V$ of highest dimension. We may always conclude that $\sum_{j\in J}(\deg W_{j})\leq(\deg V)^{2}$ , and this suffices for the main claim of the lemma. In the case that $V$ is of pure dimension, so that $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}W_{j}=\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V$ for each $j$ , then $\sum_{j\in J}(\deg W_{j})=\deg V$ , and this leads to the second conclusion of the lemma.

We proceed to prove (3.5) for irreducible $W$ , by induction on the dimension of the ambient space $\mathbb{A}^{N}$ . If $N=1$ and $W\subsetneq\mathbb{A}^{1}$ then $\#\{\mathbf{x}\in W\cap\mathbb{A}^{1}(\mathbb{Z})\}\leq\deg W$ , so that the conclusion of the lemma holds (with $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}W=0$ ). We assume the inductive hypothesis that (3.5) holds for any irreducible variety $W\subsetneq\mathbb{A}^{N-1}$ , and we prove it for any irreducible variety $V\subsetneq\mathbb{A}^{N}$ . Consider such a $V\subsetneq\mathbb{A}^{N}$ . If $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V=N-1$ so that $V$ is a hypersurface, the result of the lemma already holds by the Schwartz-Zippel trivial bound in Lemma 3.8. Thus from now on we may assume that $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V\leq N-2$ .

For each $x_{1}\in\mathbb{\mathbb{Z}}$ consider the hyperplane $H(x_{1})$ cut out by $X_{1}-x_{1}=0$ . Such hyperplanes are disjoint, i.e. $H(x_{1})\cap H(x_{1}^{\prime})=\emptyset$ if $x_{1}\neq x_{1}^{\prime}$ . Now if a hyperplane $H$ does not contain $V$ , then $V\cap H$ is a proper closed subset of $V$ and since $V$ is irreducible, $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}(V\cap H)\leq\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V-1$ . Therefore $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}(V\cap H(x_{1}))=\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V$ is possible only if $H(x_{1})$ contains $V$ but this can occur for at most one value of $x_{1}$ since the hyperplanes $\{H(x_{1})\}_{x_{1}}$ are pairwise disjoint.

Suppose now $V$ lies in (at most) one hyperplane, say $H(x_{1}^{*})$ for a fixed $x_{1}^{*}\in\mathbb{Z}$ , and for all $x_{1}\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{x_{1}^{*}\}$ , $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}(V\cap H(x_{1}))\leq\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V-1$ . Hence upon writing $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\bfy)$ for $\bfy=(x_{2},\ldots,x_{N})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V,B) \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\|\bfx\|\leq B\\
\bfx\in V\end{subarray}}1=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|x_{1}|\leq B\\
x_{1}\neq x_{1}^{*}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\|\bfy\|\leq B\\
\bfy\in V\cap H(x_{1})\end{subarray}}1+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\|\bfy\|\leq B\\
\bfy\in V\cap H(x_{1}^{*})\end{subarray}}1 \displaystyle\ll_{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V,N}(\deg V)B\cdot B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V-1}+(\deg V)B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V}. $$

Here in the first term, in the sum over $\bfy$ we have used the fact that $H(x_{1})\equiv\mathbb{A}^{N-1}$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}(V\cap H(x_{1}))\leq\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V-1\leq N-2$ , so we may apply the inductive hypothesis to the sum over $\bfy$ . In the second term, in the sum over $\bfy$ we again used $H(x_{1}^{*})\equiv\mathbb{A}^{N-1}$ , as well as the fact that we have already reduced to the case $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V\leq N-2$ . Thus even though $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}(V\cap H(x_{1}^{*}))=\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V$ , this sum over $\bfy$ is still subject to the inductive hypothesis, since $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}(V\cap H(x_{1}^{*}))\leq\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V\leq N-2<N-1$ . Thus the proof is complete. ∎

#### Remark 3.10.

Another method to achieve a bound with the exponent in Lemma 3.9 (and correspondingly in Lemma 3.1) is to apply the Lang-Weil bound (a priori stronger than the Schwartz-Zippel upper bound, since it implies a lower bound). For example, in the affine setting, consider a variety $V\subset\mathbb{A}^{N}$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ . Suppose for a given $B$ there is a prime $p\in[B/2,B]$ such that $V$ is integral over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ (and of the same dimension). Then by the Lang-Weil bound (in the affine formulation of Lemma 5.2 below), $\#V(\mathbb{F}_{p})=p^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V}+O_{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V,\deg V}(p^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V-1/2})$ . Since at most $B/p+O(1)=O(1)$ points $\mathbf{x}\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ project down to each point in $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}$ , we may conclude that $N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V,B)\ll_{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V,\deg V}p^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V}\ll B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V}.$ As stated, this bound is independent of the coefficients of the defining polynomials of $V$ , but it assumed the existence of a prime $p$ of good reduction of size comparable to $B$ . Suppose for simplicity that $V$ is a hypersurface defined as the vanishing set of a polynomial $F$ with integral coefficients, and suppose that $F$ is irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Then by a Bertini-Noether lemma (such as [BPW25, Lemma 2.9]), $F$ is irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ for all but $\ll_{N,\deg F}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ primes. In this case, the argument above would only apply as long as $B\gg\log\|F\|$ , so that $\pi(B)\gg\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ , which would imply the existence of a suitable prime $p\in[B/2,B]$ .

As a result of Lemma 3.9, for a thin set $M\subset V(\mathbb{Z})\subsetneq\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ , the trivial bound is

$$ N_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}(M,B)\ll_{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V,\deg V,n}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V}\ll B^{n-1}. $$

Pila has obtained a celebrated uniform bound: for any irreducible affine variety $V\subset\mathbb{A}^{N}$ defined over $\mathbb{R}$ of degree $d$ ,

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V,B)\ll_{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V,d,N,\varepsilon}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V-1+1/d+\varepsilon}, $$

for any $\varepsilon>0$ . See [Pil95, Thm. A]; this builds on the Bombieri-Pila argument for plane curves in [BP89]. In fact, Pila proves a stronger result, with $B^{\varepsilon}$ replaced by $\exp(12\sqrt{d\log B\log\log B})$ . Explicit refinements are now known. Cluckers, Dèbes, Hendel, Nguyen and Vermeulen [CDH+23, Prop. 2.6] quantified the dependence on $d$ in (3.7), proving

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V,B)\ll_{N}d^{e(N,\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V)}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V-1+1/d}\log B $$

for some integer $e(N,\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V)$ . In the case when $V$ is an (irreducible affine) hypersurface $H$ , Binyamini, Cluckers and Kato [BCK25, Thm. 3] showed at most quadratic dependence on degree (at the cost of more log factors), proving

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(H,B)\ll_{N}d^{2}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}H-1+1/d}(\log B)^{\gamma(N)} $$

for some $\gamma(N)\geq 0$ . By [CCDN20, Prop. 4.3.1] a result on $N_{\mathrm{aff}}(H,B)$ for hypersurfaces implies a result for $N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V,B)$ for varieties, but with an increased power of $d$ . Precisely, for each geometrically integral $V\subset\mathbb{A}^{N}$ of dimension $m$ and degree $d$ there is a geometrically integral hypersurface $H\subset\mathbb{A}^{m+1}$ (hence of dimension $m$ ) of degree $d$ and birational to $V$ such that

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V,B)\leq dN_{\mathrm{aff}}(H,c(n)d^{e(n)}B), $$

for some $c(n),e(n)$ .

The exponent in (3.7) (and the aforementioned explicit refinements) improves on Lemma 3.9 as long as $d\geq 2$ , and indeed the exponent is essentially sharp for each $d$ , as the following example shows.

#### Example 3.11.

Let $V\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ be the hypersurface defined by $F=0$ for $F(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})=X_{1}^{d}-(X_{2}+\cdots+X_{n})$ . Then $\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V=n-1$ and $N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V,B)\gg_{n,d}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V-1+1/d}$ , since

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V,B)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|z|\leq(n-1)B\\
\text{$z$ a $d$-th power}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}=z\\
(x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})\in[-B,B]^{n-1}\end{subarray}}1\gg_{n,d}B^{1/d}\cdot B^{n-2}. $$

As a consequence of this example, one could say that (3.7) concludes the study of affine thin sets of type I. However, before we conclude our investigation prematurely, let us recall that we turned to affine thin sets of type I with the promise of understanding projective thin sets of type I. We record the bridge between these settings as in [BHBS06, Thm. 1], which is proved by a birational projection argument (related to the fact that any variety $X$ of dimension $r$ is birational to a hypersurface in $\mathbb{P}^{r+1}$ , see [Har77, Ch. I Prop. 4.9]).

#### Proposition 3.12.

Consider a hypersurface $H\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ with $n\geq 3$ defined by the vanishing of a homogeneous form $F(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ of degree $d\geq 2$ that is absolutely irreducible. Let $\varepsilon>0$ . Suppose that for all such affine hypersurfaces $H$ ,

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(H,B)\ll_{n,d,\varepsilon}B^{\theta_{d,n}+\varepsilon}. $$

Then for any geometrically integral projective variety $V\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}$ of degree $d\geq 2$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V=n-2$ ,

$$ N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B)\ll_{N,d,\varepsilon}B^{\theta_{d,n}+\varepsilon}. $$

Consequently, to make progress on the Dimension Growth Conjectures 3.3 and 3.5, it suffices to sharpen Pila’s bound (3.7) only in certain cases, which exclude in particular the behavior exhibited by Example 3.11. Here is the relevant conjecture, modeled on [BHBS06, Conj. 1 and Conj. 3]. Throughout, the leading form of a polynomial is the homogeneous part of highest degree.

#### Conjecture 3.13 (Uniform Dimension Growth, affine hypersurface).

For any hypersurface $H\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ defined as the vanishing set of a polynomial $F\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ of degree $d\geq 2$ with absolutely irreducible leading form,

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(H,B)\ll_{n,d}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}H-1}s(B), $$

for a “small factor” $s(B)$ , which could take the form $s(B)\ll_{\varepsilon}B^{\varepsilon}$ (for any $\varepsilon>0$ ); or $s(B)\leq(\log B)^{\gamma(n,d)}$ for some $\gamma(n,d)>0$ ; or $s(B)\leq 1$ .

The main exponent is best possible:

#### Example 3.14.

For every $n\geq 3$ and $d\geq 2$ there exists a hypersurface $H$ with $N_{\mathrm{aff}}(H,B)\gg_{n}B^{n-2}$ . For example, consider $H\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ defined by the vanishing of $X_{1}F_{1}(\mathbf{X})-X_{2}F_{2}(\mathbf{X})$ for forms $F_{1},F_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ of degree $d-1$ ; then the form vanishes for all $(0,0,x_{3},\ldots,x_{n})$ with $|x_{j}|\leq B$ for $j=3,\ldots,n$ ; see [BHBS06, Conj. 1].

In order to apply Proposition 3.12, we need only consider the case of Conjecture 3.13 when $F$ is homogeneous, and we currently restrict our attention to this case, returning to the general setting in §3.4. When $F$ is homogeneous, Conjecture 3.13 was established by Heath-Brown for $n\leq 4$ [HB02, Thms. 3, 9] and in the cases $d=2$ , $n\geq 3$ [HB02, Thm. 2], with $s(B)\ll_{\varepsilon}B^{\varepsilon}$ for any $\varepsilon>0$ . With this same notion of small factor, Browning, Heath-Brown, and Salberger proved the conjecture in the homogeneous case for $n\geq 3$ and $d\geq 6$ [BHBS06, Cor. 2] (and certain weaker results for $3\leq d\leq 5$ ). Then Salberger [Sal23, Thm. 0.4] proved Conjecture 3.13 for all $d\geq 4$ . Cumulatively:

#### Theorem 3.15 (Browning, Heath-Brown, Salberger).

The Uniform Affine Dimension Growth Conjecture 3.13 holds for all homogeneous $F$ with degree $d\neq 3$ , with small factor $s(B)\ll_{\varepsilon}B^{\varepsilon}$ for all $\varepsilon>0$ .

It remains an open problem to verify the uniform statement in Conjecture 3.13 for $F$ homogeneous of degree $d=3$ , for example with small factor $s(B)\ll_{\varepsilon}B^{\varepsilon}$ . For degree $d=3$ , define

$$ \delta_{3}:=2/\sqrt{3}-1,\qquad\delta_{3}^{\prime}:=1/7<\delta_{3}. $$

Salberger proved that under the hypotheses of Conjecture 3.13 for $d=3$ , there is a uniform bound

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(H,B)\ll_{n,\varepsilon}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}H-1+\delta+\varepsilon}, $$

with $\delta=\delta_{3}$ obtained in [Sal23, Thm. 0.4], and the smaller value $\delta=\delta_{3}^{\prime}$ obtained in [Sal15, Thm. 16.3]; see also [Sal15, Thm. 16.4] for geometrically integral projective subvarieties. (For clarity, note that [Sal15] was developed later than, but published before, [Sal23].)

### 3.3. Type I, revisiting the projective setting

We now return to the setting of projective sets of type I. By Theorem 3.15 combined with Proposition 3.12:

#### Theorem 3.16 (Browning, Heath-Brown, Salberger).

The Uniform Dimension Growth Conjecture 3.5 holds for all cases with degree $d\neq 3$ , with $C(V)$ depending only on the dimension and degree of $V$ and with small factor $s(B)\ll_{\varepsilon}B^{\varepsilon}$ for any $\varepsilon>0$ .

As a result of (3.10), Salberger has obtained a uniform but weaker statement toward Conjecture 3.5 that for any geometrically integral variety $V\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}$ of degree 3,

$$ N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B)\ll_{\varepsilon}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V+\delta+\varepsilon}, $$

for $\delta=\delta_{3}$ [Sal23, Thm. 0.3] or the smaller $\delta=\delta_{3}^{\prime}$ [Sal15, Thm. 16.3, Cor 16.4]. It remains an open problem to improve the exponent to achieve Conjecture 3.5 for degree 3.

Salberger has also established the non-uniform Dimension Growth Conjecture for $\deg d=3$ in [Sal23, Thm. 0.1 and §8] by “ad hoc” methods (not passing through Proposition 3.12):

#### Theorem 3.17 (Salberger).

The Dimension Growth Conjecture 3.3 holds for all cases, with small factor $s(B)\ll_{\varepsilon}B^{\varepsilon}$ for any $\varepsilon>0$ .

Recent studies on Uniform Dimension Growth have further produced explicit expressions for $C(V)=C(\deg V,\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V)$ , and the small factor $s(B)$ , beginning with influential work by Walsh [Wal15], which replaced $s(B)\ll_{\varepsilon}B^{\varepsilon}$ by $s(B)\ll 1$ in a key result counting points on projective curves, underlying the approach to Theorem 3.16. Explicit refinements were continued by Castryck, Cluckers, Dittmann, Nguyen [CCDN20], who established polynomial dependence on degree in $C(V)$ .

Let us briefly motivate, at least informally, why it can be useful to make the dependence of the constant $C(V)$ on degree explicit, and to minimize it as much as possible. For example, given a geometrically integral projective hypersurface $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{r+1}$ of degree $d$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ , a version of the determinant method may produce for each $B\geq 1$ a geometrically integral hypersurface $Y_{B}$ of (potentially very large) degree $D_{Y_{B}}$ , with the properties that $X\not\subset Y_{B}$ , and all rational points on $X$ of height at most $B$ lie on $Y_{B}$ . (For example, a result of Salberger produces such a $Y_{B}$ with degree

$$ D_{Y_{B}}\ll_{d,r,\varepsilon}B^{(r+1)/(rd^{1/r})+\varepsilon}; $$

see [Sal23, Thm. 0.12]. In particular, this yields $B^{3/(2\sqrt{d})+\varepsilon}$ for $r=2$ .) Then,

$$ \{\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{Q}):H(\mathbf{x})\leq B\}\subset Y(\mathbb{Q})\implies\{\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{Q}):H(\mathbf{x})\leq B\}\subset(X\cap Y)(\mathbb{Q}). $$

Suppose from now on that $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{3}$ (that is, $r=2$ ). Now since $X\not\subset Y_{B}$ , $X\cap Y_{B}=:Z$ is a curve of degree $D_{Y_{B}}$ . Suppose now that for some function $C(\cdot)$ , it is true that for any geometrically integral curve $Z$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}\in Z(\mathbb{Q}):H(\mathbf{x})\leq B\}\ll_{\varepsilon}C(\deg Z)B^{2/\deg Z+\varepsilon}. $$

(For example, a result of Heath-Brown produces this upper bound with unspecified dependence $C(\deg Z)$ , for any geometrically integral curve in $\mathbb{P}^{3}$ [HB02, Thm. 5].) Combining these two results to answer the original question, we would arrive at a bound like

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{Q}):H(\mathbf{x})\leq B\}\ll_{\varepsilon}C(D_{Y_{B}})B^{2/D_{Y_{B}}+\varepsilon}. $$

So long as $D_{Y_{B}}$ is a function that grows to infinity with $B$ , this upper bound becomes $\ll_{\varepsilon}B^{\varepsilon}C(D_{Y_{B}})$ as $B\rightarrow\infty$ . Thus on the one hand we are motivated to show $D_{Y_{B}}\rightarrow\infty$ with $B$ , and on the other hand we need to show that the function $C(\cdot)$ is as slow-growing as possible. (For example in $\mathbb{P}^{3}$ , if $C(x)\ll x^{2}$ were quadratic and $D_{Y_{B}}\approx B^{3/(2\sqrt{d})+\varepsilon}$ , this line of reasoning would lead to an upper bound

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}\in X(\mathbb{Q}):H(\mathbf{x})\leq B\}\ll_{\varepsilon}(B^{3/2\sqrt{d}+\varepsilon})^{2}B^{2/D_{Y_{B}}+\varepsilon}\ll_{\varepsilon}B^{3/\sqrt{d}+\varepsilon}. $$

Any improvement on the degree in (3.11) would lead to a corresponding improvement here. See for example [BCS+25, Thm. 3.1, Cor 3.3], which (roughly speaking) allows $D_{Y_{B}}\ll_{d}B^{1/\sqrt{d}}(\log B)$ . Motivated by strategies like this, the goal of proving at most quadratic dependence on degree was raised by Salberger in remarks following [Sal23, Thm. 0.12].

There have been many results recently that make the dependence on degree more explicit. We record from [CCDN20, Thm. 1], for all geometrically integral varieties $V\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}$ of degree $d\geq 5$ ,

$$ N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B)\ll_{N}d^{e(N)}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V} $$

for some integer $e(N)$ . Cluckers, Dèbes, Hendel, Nguyen, Vermeulen [CDH+23, Thm. 1.2] proved $e(N)=7$ suffices if $V$ is a hypersurface. The best-known bounds show at most quadratic dependence on $d$ , due to Binyamini, Cluckers, and Novikov [BCN24] (over $\mathbb{Q}$ ) and Binyamini, Cluckers and Kato [BCK25] (including results over any global field). Precisely, as in [BCK25, Thm. 4], for any irreducible hypersurface $H$ of degree $d\geq 4$ in $\mathbb{P}^{N}$ ,

$$ N_{\mathrm{proj}}(H,B)\ll_{N}d^{2}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}H}(\log B)^{\gamma(N)} $$

for some $\gamma(N)$ , while for degree $d=3$ ,

$$ N_{\mathrm{proj}}(H,B)\ll_{N}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}H+\delta_{3}}(\log B)^{\gamma(N)}, $$

for $\delta_{3}$ as in (3.9). It remains an open problem to improve the exponent to $\dim_{\mathbb{P}}H$ for degree $3$ . These results for hypersurfaces imply results for varieties, but with an increased power of $d$ : by [CCDN20, Prop. 4.3.2], for each geometrically integral $V\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{P}}V=m$ and degree $d$ there is a geometrically integral hypersurface $H\subset\mathbb{P}^{m+1}$ (hence of dimension $m$ ) of degree $d$ and birational to $V$ such that

$$ N_{\mathrm{proj}}(V,B)\leq dN_{\mathrm{proj}}(H,c(n)d^{e(n)}B) $$

for some $c(n),e(n)$ .

As noted in [CCDN20, §1.4], by Example 3.4, (3.12) cannot be true in general for degree $d=2$ . It remains open whether a bound with small factor $s(B)\ll 1$ could be true for degrees $d=3,4$ .

Lower bounds have also been studied. By [CCDN20, §6], for every degree $d\geq 1$ there is a geometrically integral degree $d$ hypersurface $H\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}$ such that $N_{\mathrm{proj}}(H,B)\gg_{N}dB^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}H}$ , so that in general one cannot expect to achieve smaller than linear growth in $d$ . This has been improved by Cluckers and Glazer [CG25, Thm. 2] to the statement that quadratic growth in $d$ is “eventually tight” (as $N\rightarrow\infty$ ). More precisely, for any $N\geq 2$ and $B_{0}\geq 1$ , there exists $c(N)>0$ , $B\geq B_{0}$ and $d>B_{0}$ , and an integral hypersurface $H\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}$ of degree $d$ such that

$$ N_{\mathrm{proj}}(H,B)\geq c(N)d^{2-2/N}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{P}}H}. $$

It remains an open question to understand the small discrepancy in dependence on degree, compared to the upper bound (3.13); here very recent work of Dehennin is making progress [Deh26].

### 3.4. Type I, revisiting the affine setting

We now revisit the affine setting of Dimension Growth results. We have observed in Example 3.11 that the exponent in Pila’s bound (3.7) cannot be improved if $V\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ is allowed to be an arbitrary irreducible variety, although Theorem 3.15 improves it when $V$ is a hypersurface defined as the vanishing set of an absolutely irreducible form $F$ (of degree $d\neq 3$ ). It is natural to ask for the largest class of “allowable” affine varieties $V\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ of degree $d\geq 2$ for which can (3.7) be improved to

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(V,B)\leq C(n,d)B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}V-1}s(B), $$

for a suitable small factor $s(B)$ , in the terminology of Conjecture 3.13. We turn now to progress on this question.

#### 3.4.1. Hypersurfaces

We first consider the setting where $V$ is a hypersurface $H$ . Salberger achieved (3.15) (with $s(B)\ll_{\varepsilon}B^{\varepsilon}$ for every $\varepsilon>0$ ) for any affine hypersurface $H\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ defined as the vanishing set of a polynomial $f\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ of degree $d\geq 4$ and $n\geq 3$ , with leading form (homogeneous part of highest degree) that is absolutely irreducible, hence verifying Conjecture 3.13 in these cases [Sal23, Thm. 0.4]. (We believe the hypothesis of that theorem intended to require absolute irreducibility, as for example in [Sal23, Thm. 7.4].) To interpret this condition geometrically, if $f$ is a polynomial of degree $d$ in $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ , let $F(T,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ denote its homogenization. Then to say the leading form $f_{d}$ of $f$ is absolutely irreducible is to say that the intersection of the homogenization $F(T,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})=0$ with the plane at infinity $\{T=0\}$ is geometrically irreducible, since $V(F)\cap V(T)=V(f_{d})$ .

It remains an open problem to prove an analogous result when $f$ has degree $d=3$ , with leading form that is absolutely irreducible. Instead, Salberger has proved

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(H,B)\ll_{n,\varepsilon}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}H-1+\delta+\varepsilon}, $$

with $\delta=\delta_{3}$ as in (3.9) obtained in [Sal23, Thm. 0.4], and the smaller value $\delta=\delta_{3}^{\prime}$ obtained in [Sal15, Thm. 16.3]. Dependence on degree in (3.15) for $V$ a hypersurface has been made explicit by [BCN24] and [BCK25]: as in [BCK25, Thm. 5], one may take $C(n,d)\ll_{n}d^{2}$ and $s(B)\leq(\log B)^{\gamma(n)}$ for some constant $\gamma(n)$ , for degree $d\geq 4$ ; while if $d=3$ , they obtain

$$ N_{\mathrm{aff}}(H,B)\ll_{n}B^{\dim_{\mathbb{A}}H-1+\delta_{3}}(\log B)^{\gamma(n)}. $$

Next, consider the case where $V$ is a hypersurface $H$ , but we aim to relax the condition that the leading form of the defining polynomial of $H$ is absolutely irreducible. The work [CDH+23] replaces this with a condition that the hypersurface is not cylindrical over a curve (NCC). Precisely, as in [CDH+23, Dfn. 1.3], a hypersurface $H\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ is said to be cylindrical over a curve if there exists a $\mathbb{Q}$ -linear map $L:\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Q})\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{2}(\mathbb{Q})$ and a curve $C$ in $\mathbb{A}^{2}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $H=L^{-1}(C)$ . Otherwise, $H$ is not cylindrical over a curve. A polynomial $f\in\mathbb{Q}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ is said to be NCC precisely when the hypersurface $H\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}$ defined as the vanishing set $V(f)$ is NCC.

#### Remark 3.18 (On being cylindrical over a curve).

As remarked in [CDH+23], the property that a polynomial $f$ is cylindrical over a curve is equivalent to saying there exists a polynomial $g\in\mathbb{Q}[Y_{1},Y_{2}]$ and linear forms $L_{1}(\mathbf{X}),L_{2}(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Q}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ such that $f(\mathbf{X})=g(L_{1}(\mathbf{X}),L_{2}(\mathbf{X}))$ . If this holds, then by a $\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ change of variables, $f(\mathbf{X})$ can be made to depend on (at most) two variables.
